This post may be disturbing for those with trypophobia. Click here to view the rest of this post.

Similar to the box, I was very excited for this project. Unfortunately, I attempted something far too complex, achieved very disappointing results, and only produced one object of the five that I was to make.

My theme for this semester is Art Deco, which is a uniquely American architectural style that emphasizes polychromatic coloring, exaggerated human forms, setback reliefs, and clocks. For this project, I specifically focused on Ziggurat like reliefs, which means there are lots of setbacks in the building. The Empire State Building and the American Radiator are classic examples of this style. That being said, I was not willing to make an entire building or even a model of one, so I decided to make a saucer, where instead of a curve, it was as though you were trying to make a curved base with only 4 angles.

This idea was entirely my own, but came after some deliberation in ChatGPTSaucer design conversation. Below are some drawings I made, which I gave as context to Codex:

Along with ideation, Codex was especially useful for generating a Blender file that allowed me to visualize what I had in mind and made it easy to play around with my assumptions. The Blender file looked like this:

In mind, the process for this was fairly simple: I would measure out each recessed section, each increasing in length and depth as they got closer to the base (see above for exact dimensions), draw lines, and then use the drill press to make the various sections.

In practice, I not only struggled immensely with drawing straight lines, the drilling process took over 100 holes and an amount of precision I did not possess. Additionally, while you were very helpful in terms of figuring out how to make precise the drilling process, I found it very difficult to actually eyeball the exact place the drill was at all times. As a result, the saucer has clear levels, but which are incredibly uneven.

The below is a GIF of the various jigs I made simply to draw the lines, which ended up being dramatically uneven despite this Rube Goldberg-esque process.

After drilling the recesses in, the “saucer” I made was incredibly uneven and filled with holes. This was planned for, and I tried my hand at two types of Dremels, one sandpaper and one metal, to even things out. This was the most satisfying part of this process, and it gave my woodwork some resemblance to what was created in Blender. Still, the result is quite rough.

I am sorry that I did not get to create all 5. At 9:45PM today I had the idea of using clippers and saws to make the recessed levels, which would have possibly produced a more precise and aesthetically pleasing result. Unfortunately, I lacked the willpower to stay up to finish out all 5.

This process has been a humbling lesson in the limits of converting imagination to reality. Still, I know this project would have been possible with access and knowledge of how to use a CNC machine, which I will perhaps do to redeem myself in the future.

I remain incredibly excited for future projects in this class.
